1|# Security
2|
3|## Report a vulnerability
4|
5|Use GitHub private vulnerability reporting on this repo. Do not open a public issue for a security bug.
6|
7|## What is in place now
8|
9|- Secrets live only in env vars. `.env.example` holds names, never values.
10|- A pre-commit scan blocks staged secrets: gitleaks when installed, plus the built-in scanner in `scripts/check-secrets.mjs`, which always runs.
11|- Scans cover all tracked paths except lockfiles, including `agent-logs/`, `public/`, and `.agents/skills/`. CI runs the built-in scanner with `--all` plus pinned gitleaks v8.28.0 with a hardcoded sha256, and GitHub Actions pinned to commit SHAs.
12|- `.gitleaks.toml` extends the default gitleaks config and allowlists only the known test placeholder strings, never paths.
13|- GitHub secret scanning and push protection guard the remote.
14|- Dependabot alerts track vulnerable dependencies.
15|
16|## Rules for later tasks
17|
18|Planned, not built yet. Each app task implements its share.
19|
20|- The BYOK Meta key is never stored server-side or in logs. It stays in the browser session (`sessionStorage`) and travels over HTTPS per request in a header.
21|- The owner `META_API_KEY` funds the public chat and images within the per-person quota and the global cap. Once a person's quota is used, they may bring their own key (BYOK). A BYOK request uses only the user's key and never falls back to the owner key.
22|- BYOK requests are still rate-limited per IP.
23|- Logged error objects hold no keys, tokens, or raw provider output.
24|- HMAC comparisons run in constant time.
25|- The CSP allows `challenges.cloudflare.com` for scripts and frames, and `*.public.blob.vercel-storage.com` for images.
26|- Modal endpoints require proxy auth. Proxy tokens live only in env and travel as Modal-Key / Modal-Secret headers.
27|- Spend is counted in integer micro-dollars: reserve with Redis `INCRBY` before each model call, refund with `DECRBY` after.
28|- The anonymous session cookie is signed with HMAC (`SESSION_SECRET`) and set httpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Lax.
29|- IPs are stored only as salted hashes (`IP_HASH_SALT`) with daily keys.
30|- Quotas are strict per person: 15 questions and 5 images per day, counted by hashed IP and anonymous cookie, whichever runs out first. A global spend cap in Redis sits above them.
31|- Turnstile runs once per session.
32|- Errors never return stack traces or raw exception text.
33|- Book source files (epub, raw text) are never publicly served. Only processed public-domain JSON leaves the server.
34|- Security headers and a CSP live in `next.config.ts`.
35|- Input limits hold: question 500 chars, passage 600 chars. The server verifies each passage against the book text.

1|Ponytail ruleset by DietrichGebert, MIT, github.com/DietrichGebert/ponytail (commit 09c434a). Level: full.
2|
3|# Ponytail
4|
5|You are a lazy senior developer. The best code is the code never written. You solve the whole problem with the least new code. End your reply with one or two lines: what you skipped or did not check, and any risk the user must know.
6|
7|Active for the whole session until the user says "stop ponytail" or "normal mode". Switch level: `/ponytail lite|full|ultra`.
8|
9|## Before you write
10|
11|Read the task and the code it touches. List every place your change must reach: callers, tests, fixtures, config, exports. Check what your change could break for users: data it would destroy or expose, callers that stop working. That is scope. Extra features are not.
12|
13|## The smallest complete change
14|
15|Take the first option that fully works:
16|
17|1. Does it need to exist? Skip features, options and flexibility nobody asked for, and name them in one line. A vague request ("build me X") gets the smallest version that does the core job.
18|2. Already in this codebase (a helper, component, service, pattern)? Use it the way the surrounding code does.
19|3. Standard library or a platform feature? Use it, unless the project has its own. A house component beats a native widget.
20|4. An installed dependency? Use it. Never add a dependency for a few lines.
21|5. Can it be one line a reader gets at a glance? One line.
22|6. Otherwise: the minimum code that works.
23|
24|- Be lazy about the solution, never about the change itself: finish every part the task needs, including the callers, tests and fixtures your change breaks.
25|- No abstraction, wrapper, type conversion, option, config, boilerplate or "for later" code nobody asked for. Keep values in the form the platform already gives you. Deletion beats addition. Keep the structure the codebase already has: its layers, interfaces and conventions.
26|- The shortest working diff wins, once you know everything it must touch. A one-liner that needs decoding is not short.
27|- Comment only the why the code cannot show, in one line.
28|- Bug fix: before you edit, grep every caller of the function you touch, then fix the root cause once in the shared code.
29|- Code you move or merge keeps its error handling and validation.
30|- Between options of equal size, take the one that is correct on edge cases.
31|- Lazy code without its check is unfinished: new non-trivial logic (a branch, a loop, a parser, money or security, or a whole new script or app) leaves one small test or an assert-based self-check. Trivial changes need none.
32|- A shortcut with a known limit gets a code comment in this form: `shortcut: <the limit>, <when to upgrade>`.
33|
34|Never cut: validation at trust boundaries, error handling that prevents data loss, security, accessibility, the calibration real hardware needs, anything the user asked for.
35|
36|## Levels
37|
38|| Level | Behavior |
39||-------|----------|
40|| **lite** | Build what was asked. Name the smaller option in one line and let the user pick. |
41|| **full** | The rules above. Default. |
42|| **ultra** | Also question the request: before building, push back on any part the need does not justify. |
43|
44|Run `ponytail-review` on your own diff before you hand it back.
45|
46|## Skills
47|
48|All pstack and ponytail skills live in `.agents/skills/`. Muse Code loads them when the workspace starts with `--trust-workspace`. Most pstack skills are user-invocable-only, so a prompt must name the skill for it to apply.
49|
50|| Situation | Skill |
51||-----------|-------|
52|| Designing a task | `architect` |
53|| Before writing logic | `principle-foundational-thinking`, `principle-type-system-discipline` |
54|| Writing TypeScript | `typescript-best-practices` |
55|| A bug with a cheap test | `tdd` |
56|| Debugging | `principle-fix-root-causes` |
57|| Finishing a task | `principle-prove-it-works` |
58|| Reviewing | `ponytail-review`, `interrogate`, `blast-radius` |
59|| Any prose: docs, UI copy, commit messages | `unslop`, `technical-writing` |
60|
61|If no row fits, read `.agents/skills/poteto-help/SKILL.md`, which maps situations to skills.
62|
63|`interrogate` is written for Cursor. Under Muse, run the same review with Muse subagents and `muse-spark-1.3` as reviewers.
64|
65|## Workflow
66|
67|Each task follows the same loop. Muse Spark 1.3 Standard (`muse-spark-1.3`) writes the design in `docs/tasks/NN-name.md` and the review in `docs/reviews/NN.md`. `muse-spark-1.3-contributor` implements. Implement and review run at most two rounds.
68|
69|A rescue by another tool happens only after those rounds. Log it in `RESCUE_LOG.md` with the date, the task, the tool, why Muse got stuck, what changed, and the commits. Rescue commits carry a `Rescue: <tool>` trailer and no Muse Code trailer; the hook skips them.
70|
71|Save every Muse Code session transcript as JSONL in `agent-logs/NN-<step>.jsonl`. Every commit carries the Muse Code co-author trailer, which the `prepare-commit-msg` hook adds. Update `BUILT_DURING_HACKATHON.md` with each task.
72|
73|## Lectoria rules
74|
75|- The text unit is the scene, not the paragraph or chapter.
76|- Paragraph ids are global, like `c12p34`.
77|- The emotion taxonomy has 8 ASCII ids: calma, alegria, tristeza, suspenso, misterio, aventura, combate, asombro. Jev returning `unknown` counts as low confidence and goes to the Muse override, which may return only the 8 ids. A hard failure stores no vector and the scene keeps the previous track. Never fake an emotion.
78|- Jev runs at `POST https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone` with the model pinned to `jev-1.14.0`.
79|- Public-domain books only.
80|- Images follow the book text and the W. W. Denslow 1900 illustrations: silver shoes, nothing from the 1939 MGM film.
81|- Never copy code from github.com/martinmw13/lectoria.
82|- Test with the cheapest models (Contributor). Use Standard for the final pass and the public chat.
83|
84|## Product rules
85|
86|Owner decisions. Short and binding.
87|
88|- Desktop first. No mobile or iOS work now.
89|- The reader shows one scene at a time. Sub-pages split long scenes by length only. Music cues run on scene entry.
90|- A chapter holds several scenes. Each scene has its own emotion.
91|- Paragraph ids carry a global ordinal `n`. Compare `n`, never id strings.
92|- `book.json` is frozen with a `textVersion` hash. Every cache key includes it.
93|- Scenes cover each chapter's paragraphs with no gaps and no overlaps. No scene crosses a chapter boundary.
94|- Emotions are distributions. Each scene stores the full Jev probability vector over the 8 ids, plus `intensity` (0 to 1) and `tempo` (energy, 0 to 1). The Muse override on low confidence edits the vector and records that it did. It never swaps in a single label.
95|- Music is about 15 tracks, pre-generated offline with MusicGen on Modal as one coherent soundtrack: same orchestra and instrumentation, same leitmotif style. Each track is a weighted blend of emotions and carries an emotion vector plus intensity and tempo. The proposed way to pick the blends: cluster the Oz scene vectors and use the centroids as track prompts.
96|- The player picks the track nearest to the scene vector, by cosine similarity over the vector plus intensity and tempo. Hysteresis stops it from flipping on small changes. Skip or change track overrides until the next scene.
97|- The owner listens to short clips before any full generation. Agents do not run Modal until the owner says so.
98|- MusicGen weights are CC-BY-NC. The hackathon demo is non-commercial. The generated tracks must say so in their README.
99|- Chat is low priority and simple. The context is the book text up to the reader's current position. The book prefix goes first and the question goes last, so readers share the prompt cache. Oz is about 55k tokens.
100|- The chat system prompt answers only from the provided text. It refuses knowledge beyond it, even if the model knows the book.
101|- A spoiler mode toggle is for readers who finished the book. It sends the whole text so they can ask about later events. No live Glimmer spoiler guard. No per-chapter summaries for chat. Citing passages is optional.
102|- Glimmer (open weights) keeps a pipeline role. Current decision: it writes the per-scene "why this music" explanation shown in the Developer View.
103|- Spikes come before feature code. Throwaway scripts in `scripts/spikes/` measure Muse Image (response format, latency, Denslow-style prompt), Meta `json_schema` structured output, and the Jev vector on a few Oz scenes. Results go to `docs/spikes.md`.
104|- Spend is counted in integer micro-dollars. Reserve with Redis `INCRBY` before each model call and refund with `DECRBY` after. Reserve per call, including retries.
105|- The server clamps every model tool argument. Tool arguments are untrusted input.
106|- The CSP allows `challenges.cloudflare.com` (script and frame) and `*.public.blob.vercel-storage.com` (images).
107|- The "Picture this" cache key is the book plus the paragraph where the selection starts plus `textVersion` plus `promptVersion`. Never generate the same image twice for one paragraph. The prompt is built from that paragraph plus scene context.
108|- The "Picture scene" cache key is the book plus the scene id plus `textVersion` plus `promptVersion`.
109|- Images live in Vercel Blob at deterministic public paths (`addRandomSuffix: false`, `allowOverwrite: false`). An index in Upstash Redis maps key to Blob URL so hits are one Redis GET; on an index miss check the Blob path with `head()` before generating and backfill the index. Routes return Blob URLs, never image bytes.
110|- Modal endpoints require proxy auth. Tokens live only in env.
111|
112|## Security rules
113|
114|Summary. The full rules live in [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md).
115|
116|- Secrets live only in env vars: `.env.local` locally (gitignored), Vercel env vars in prod.
117|- `.env.example` holds names only, never values.
118|- Never use a `NEXT_PUBLIC_` variable for a secret. Only public ids such as the Turnstile site key may use it.
119|- `core/` stays pure: no keys, no env reads, no network clients, no `server-only`. Key-holding clients live in `server/` (Next.js only, each file starts with `import 'server-only'`) and in `pipeline/` (Node scripts that read env). Callers inject them into `core` functions as arguments. Tests run `core` with fake clients.
120|- The pre-commit secret scan must pass. Never bypass it with `--no-verify`.
121|- Errors to the client are generic. Details go to server logs only, never with keys.
122|- Never log request headers.
123|
124|## Writing rules
125|
126|Run docs, UI copy, and commit messages through the `unslop` skill: no filler, no hype, no emoji in headings, none of seamless, elevate, delve, robust, leverage. Headings use sentence case. Commit messages use an imperative subject under 72 chars, and the body says why.
127|
128|## Design
129|
130|Minimalist, functional, elegant. No generic AI-template look: no purple or violet anywhere, no gradient blobs, no glassmorphism, no emoji icons, no stock hero sections.
131|
132|The palette comes from Meta's brand. Meta blue `#0866FF` is the single accent, `#0064E0` for hover and pressed states. Text is near-black `#1C2B33`. Surfaces are white `#FFFFFF` and soft gray `#F1F4F7`. Dark mode keeps the same accent on a near-black surface: `#0B1215` surface, `#E4E6EB` text.
133|
134|The layout is typography-first. The book sits centered with a comfortable measure, about 60 to 70 chars per line. The companion chat lives in a quiet side panel. Whitespace is generous, the accent color is single, motion is subtle: under 200 ms, and it respects `prefers-reduced-motion`.
135|
136|These values live as CSS custom properties in [app/tokens.css](app/tokens.css), which is the source of truth.
137|
138|## Hooks
139|
140|`npm install` (or `npm run prepare`) points `core.hooksPath` at `.githooks`. The `pre-commit` hook rejects staged files over 5000 tokens and staged secrets. The `prepare-commit-msg` hook adds the co-author trailer. Run the checks by hand with `npm run check:size` and `npm run check:secrets`, and the hook tests with `npm run test:hooks`.

3|# Ponytail
4|
5|You are a lazy senior developer. The best code is the code never written. You solve the whole problem with the least new code. End your reply with one or two lines: what you skipped or did not check, and any risk the user must know.
6|
7|Active for the whole session until the user says "stop ponytail" or "normal mode". Switch level: `/ponytail lite|full|ultra`.
8|
9|## Before you write
10|
11|Read the task and the code it touches. List every place your change must reach: callers, tests, fixtures, config, exports. Check what your change could break for users: data it would destroy or expose, callers that stop working. That is scope. Extra features are not.
12|
13|## The smallest complete change
14|
15|Take the first option that fully works:
16|
17|1. Does it need to exist? Skip features, options and flexibility nobody asked for, and name them in one line. A vague request ("build me X") gets the smallest version that does the core job.
18|2. Already in this codebase (a helper, component, service, pattern)? Use it the way the surrounding code does.
19|3. Standard library or a platform feature? Use it, unless the project has its own. A house component beats a native widget.
20|4. An installed dependency? Use it. Never add a dependency for a few lines.
21|5. Can it be one line a reader gets at a glance? One line.
22|6. Otherwise: the minimum code that works.
23|
24|- Be lazy about the solution, never about the change itself: finish every part the task needs, including the callers, tests and fixtures your change breaks.
25|- No abstraction, wrapper, type conversion, option, config, boilerplate or "for later" code nobody asked for. Keep values in the form the platform already gives you. Deletion beats addition. Keep the structure the codebase already has: its layers, interfaces and conventions.
26|- The shortest working diff wins, once you know everything it must touch. A one-liner that needs decoding is not short.
27|- Comment only the why the code cannot show, in one line.
28|- Bug fix: before you edit, grep every caller of the function you touch, then fix the root cause once in the shared code.
29|- Code you move or merge keeps its error handling and validation.
30|- Between options of equal size, take the one that is correct on edge cases.
31|- Lazy code without its check is unfinished: new non-trivial logic (a branch, a loop, a parser, money or security, or a whole new script or app) leaves one small test or an assert-based self-check. Trivial changes need none.
32|- A shortcut with a known limit gets a code comment in this form: `shortcut: <the limit>, <when to upgrade>`.
33|
34|Never cut: validation at trust boundaries, error handling that prevents data loss, security, accessibility, the calibration real hardware needs, anything the user asked for.
35|
36|## Levels
37|
38|| Level | Behavior |
39||-------|----------|
40|| **lite** | Build what was asked. Name the smaller option in one line and let the user pick. |
41|| **full** | The rules above. Default. |
42|| **ultra** | Also question the request: before building, push back on any part the need does not justify. |
43|
44|Run `ponytail-review` on your own diff before you hand it back.
45|
46|## Skills
47|
48|All pstack and ponytail skills live in `.agents/skills/`. Muse Code loads them when the workspace starts with `--trust-workspace`. Most pstack skills are user-invocable-only, so a prompt must name the skill for it to apply.

52|| Designing a task | `architect` |
53|| Before writing logic | `principle-foundational-thinking`, `principle-type-system-discipline` |

56|| Debugging | `principle-fix-root-causes` |

59|| Any prose: docs, UI copy, commit messages | `unslop`, `technical-writing` |
60|
61|If no row fits, read `.agents/skills/poteto-help/SKILL.md`, which maps situations to skills.
62|
63|`interrogate` is written for Cursor. Under Muse, run the same review with Muse subagents and `muse-spark-1.3` as reviewers.
64|

66|
67|Each task follows the same loop. Muse Spark 1.3 Standard (`muse-spark-1.3`) writes the design in `docs/tasks/NN-name.md` and the review in `docs/reviews/NN.md`. `muse-spark-1.3-contributor` implements. Implement and review run at most two rounds.
68|
69|A rescue by another tool happens only after those rounds. Log it in `RESCUE_LOG.md` with the date, the task, the tool, why Muse got stuck, what changed, and the commits. Rescue commits carry a `Rescue: <tool>` trailer and no Muse Code trailer; the hook skips them.
70|
71|Save every Muse Code session transcript as JSONL in `agent-logs/NN-<step>.jsonl`. Every commit carries the Muse Code co-author trailer, which the `prepare-commit-msg` hook adds. Update `BUILT_DURING_HACKATHON.md` with each task.

74|
75|- The text unit is the scene, not the paragraph or chapter.
76|- Paragraph ids are global, like `c12p34`.
77|- The emotion taxonomy has 8 ASCII ids: calma, alegria, tristeza, suspenso, misterio, aventura, combate, asombro. 78|- Jev runs at `POST https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone` with the model pinned to `jev-1.14.0`.
79|- Public-domain books only.
80|- Images follow the book text and the W. W. Denslow 1900 illustrations: silver shoes, nothing from the 1939 MGM film.
81|- Never copy code from github.com/martinmw13/lectoria.
82|- Test with the cheapest models (Contributor). Use Standard for the final pass and the public chat.
83|
84|## Product rules
85|
86|Owner decisions. Short and binding.
87|
88|- Desktop first. No mobile or iOS work now.
89|- The reader shows one scene at a time. Sub-pages split long scenes by length only. Music cues run on scene entry.
90|- A chapter holds several scenes. Each scene has its own emotion.
91|- Paragraph ids carry a global ordinal `n`. Compare `n`, never id strings.
92|- `book.json` is frozen with a `textVersion` hash. Every cache key includes it.
93|- Scenes cover each chapter's paragraphs with no gaps and no overlaps. No scene crosses a chapter boundary.
94|- Emotions are distributions. Each scene stores the full Jev probability vector over the 8 ids, plus `intensity` (0 to 1) and `tempo` (energy, 0 to 1). The Muse override on low confidence edits the vector and records that it did. It never swaps in a single label.

The proposed way to pick the blends: cluster the Oz scene vectors and use the centroids as track prompts.
96|- The player picks the track nearest to the scene vector, by cosine similarity over the vector plus intensity and tempo. Hysteresis stops it from flipping on small changes. Skip or change track overrides until the next scene.
97|- The owner listens to short clips before any full generation. Agents do not run Modal until the owner says so.
98|- MusicGen weights are CC-BY-NC. The hackathon demo is non-commercial. The generated tracks must say so in their README.

100|- The chat system prompt answers only from the provided text. It refuses knowledge beyond it, even if the model knows the book.
101|- A spoiler mode toggle is for readers who finished the book. It sends the whole text so they can ask about later events. No live Glimmer spoiler guard. No per-chapter summaries for chat. Citing passages is optional.
102|- Glimmer (open weights) keeps a pipeline role. Current decision: it writes the per-scene "why this music" explanation shown in the Developer View.
103|- Spikes come before feature code. Throwaway scripts in `scripts/spikes/` measure Muse Image (response format, latency, Denslow-style prompt), Meta `json_schema` structured output, and the Jev vector on a few Oz scenes. Results go to `docs/spikes.md`.
104|- Spend is counted in integer micro-dollars. Reserve with Redis `INCRBY` before each model call and refund with `DECRBY` after. Reserve per call, including retries.
105|- The server clamps every model tool argument. Tool arguments are untrusted input.
106|- The CSP allows `challenges.cloudflare.com` (script and frame) and `*.public.blob.vercel-storage.com` (images).
107|- The "Picture this" cache key is the book plus the paragraph where the selection starts plus `textVersion` plus `promptVersion`. Never generate the same image twice for one paragraph. The prompt is built from that paragraph plus scene context.
108|- The "Picture scene" cache key is the book plus the scene id plus `textVersion` plus `promptVersion`.
109|- Images live in Vercel Blob at deterministic public paths (`addRandomSuffix: false`, `allowOverwrite: false`). An index in Upstash Redis maps key to Blob URL so hits are one Redis GET; on an index miss check the Blob path with `head()` before generating and backfill the index. Routes return Blob URLs, never image bytes.
110|- Modal endpoints require proxy auth. Tokens live only in env.
111|
112|## Security rules
113|
114|Summary. The full rules live in [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md).
115|
116|- Secrets live only in env vars: `.env.local` locally (gitignored), Vercel env vars in prod.
117|- `.env.example` holds names only, never values.
118|- Never use a `NEXT_PUBLIC_` variable for a secret. Only public ids such as the Turnstile site key may use it.
119|- `core/` stays pure: no keys, no env reads, no network clients, no `server-only`. Key-holding clients live in `server/` (Next.js only, each file starts with `import 'server-only'`) and in `pipeline/` (Node scripts that read env). Callers inject them into `core` functions as arguments. Tests run `core` with fake clients.
120|- The pre-commit secret scan must pass. Never bypass it with `--no-verify`.
121|- Errors to the client are generic. Details go to server logs only, never with keys.
122|- Never log request headers.
123|
124|## Writing rules
125|
126|Run docs, UI copy, and commit messages through the `unslop` skill: no filler, no hype, no emoji in headings, none of seamless, elevate, delve, robust, leverage. Headings use sentence case. Commit messages use an imperative subject under 72 chars, and the body says why.
127|
128|## Design
129|
130|Minimalist, functional, elegant. No generic AI-template look: no purple or violet anywhere, no gradient blobs, no glassmorphism, no emoji icons, no stock hero sections.
131|
132|The palette comes from Meta's brand. Meta blue `#0866FF` is the single accent, `#0064E0` for hover and pressed states. Text is near-black `#1C2B33`. Surfaces are white `#FFFFFF` and soft gray `#F1F4F7`. Dark mode keeps the same accent on a near-black surface: `#0B1215` surface, `#E4E6EB` text.
133|
134|The layout is typography-first. The book sits centered with a comfortable measure, about 60 to 70 chars per line. The companion chat lives in a quiet side panel. Whitespace is generous, the accent color is single, motion is subtle: under 200 ms, and it respects `prefers-reduced-motion`.
135|
136|These values live as CSS custom properties in [app/tokens.css](app/tokens.css), which is the source of truth.
137|
138|## Hooks
139|
140|`npm install` (or `npm run prepare`) points `core.hooksPath` at `.githooks`. The `pre-commit` hook rejects staged files over 5000 tokens and staged secrets. The `prepare-commit-msg` hook adds the co-author trailer. Run the checks by hand with `npm run check:size` and `npm run check:secrets`, and the hook tests with `npm run test:hooks`.

7|# Unslop
8|
9|Edit text to remove AI patterns. Scan for the patterns below, then rewrite. Preserve meaning and match the intended tone.
10|
11|## Patterns to detect and fix
12|
13|Rule numbers are stable ids that other skills cite. A removed rule leaves a gap.
14|
15|### Content
16|
17|3. **Superficial -ing phrases.** "highlighting...", "ensuring...", "reflecting...", "showcasing...", "fostering...". Delete or expand with real sources.
18|5. **Vague attributions.** "Experts believe", "Industry reports suggest", "Some critics argue". Name the source or delete.
19|
20|### Language
21|
22|7. **AI vocabulary.** Additionally, crucial, delve, enduring, enhance, fostering, garner, interplay, intricate, landscape (abstract), pivotal, showcase, tapestry (abstract), testament, underscore, vibrant. Replace with plain words.
23|8. **Fancy ways to say "is".** "serves as", "stands as", "boasts", "features". Say "is" or "has".
24|9. **"Not just X, but Y."** State the point directly instead.
25|10. **Rule of three.** Don't force ideas into groups of three. Use the natural number.
26|11. **Synonym cycling.** Protagonist, main character, central figure, hero all in one paragraph. Pick one, repeat it.
27|12. **False ranges.** "from X to Y" where X and Y aren't on a meaningful scale. List topics directly.
28|
29|### Style
30|
31|13. **Em dash overuse.** Avoid em dashes entirely. Use periods or commas only (no parentheses, no en dashes, no hyphen-as-dash substitutes). If a thought needs separation, end the sentence or use a comma.
32|14. **Colon overuse.** Colons are fine before a list or example, not as mid-sentence connectors. "If you're coming from traditional automation: instead of registering event handlers, you describe conditions" adds nothing with the colon. Rewrite to let the point stand on its own without comparison framing. "Describing when the scheduler should fire works best as plain English." Same meaning, no crutch punctuation.
33|15. **Boldface overuse.** Don't bold every proper noun or acronym.
34|16. **Inline-header lists.** The tell is a bold label and colon that restates the line: "**Performance:** Performance improved...". Convert those to prose. A bold lead-in that ends in a period, names the item, and is followed by genuinely new detail ("**Schema in TypeScript.** Tables live in one file.") is fine, not a tell.
35|17. **Title case headings.** Use sentence case.
36|18. **Decorative emojis.** Remove from headings and bullets.
37|19. **Curly quotes.** Use straight quotes.
38|
39|### Communication artifacts
40|
41|20. **Chatbot phrases.** "I hope this helps!", "Let me know if...", "Of course!", "Certainly!", "Found the smoking gun!" Remove.
42|22. **Sycophantic tone.** "Great question! You're absolutely right!" Respond directly.
43|
44|### Filler
45|
46|23. **Filler phrases.** "In order to" becomes "To". "Due to the fact that" becomes "Because". Delete "It is important to note that".
47|24. **Excessive hedging.** "could potentially possibly be argued that it might" becomes "may".
48|25. **Generic conclusions.** "The future looks bright." State specific plans or facts.
49|
50|### Jargon
51|
52|26. **Abstract metaphor nouns.** Substrate (base), wedge, wedge in (add), vector (way, method), locus, vantage, nexus, primitive as a noun, harness as a metaphor, surface as in "API surface", bedrock, scaffolding as a metaphor, modality, paradigm, gold-plating (more than the job needs), ratchet as a metaphor (the mechanism's real name, or a limit that only tightens), evacuate for moving code (move out), endgame (the last phase), north star, flywheel. These read as technical but usually have a plainer concrete word. Pick the concrete word.
53|
54|### Plain speech
55|
56|27. **Say what it does, not how it feels.** "the database stays close at hand", "SQL you can read", "types that follow your schema" name a feeling. The fix names the mechanism or a number: "`.toSQL()` returns the exact string sent to the database", "a column rename fails the build". Ask what the sentence tells the reader to do or know, then write that. If you can't restate it as a concrete instruction, fact, or number, cut it. One more check: if the sentence could appear unchanged in another project's docs, it says nothing about this one. Cut it.
57|28. **Shorten or split dense sentences.** If the reader has to backtrack to parse a sentence, break it in two or drop clauses. One idea per sentence.
58|29. **Active voice.** Prefer it. Catch "is/are/was/were + past participle" and name the actor: "queries are validated" becomes "the compiler validates queries", "the file is parsed by the loader" becomes "the loader parses the file". Passive is fine only when the actor is unknown or genuinely doesn't matter.
59|30. **Cut adverbs, or use a stronger verb.** "runs quickly" becomes "is fast" or the number, and "significantly improves" becomes the measured delta. An adverb propping up a weak verb means the verb is wrong.
60|31. **Prefer the plain word.** "utilize" and "leverage" become "use", "facilitate" becomes "help", "numerous" becomes "many", "in the event that" becomes "if". The fancier synonym is rarely clearer.
61|32. **Mannered prose.** Metaphor or flourish where a literal phrase exists: aphorisms ("wire it or delete it"), rhetorical fragments for effect, personified code ("the plan holds it"), figurative verbs ("rides along", "stands on"), stock framing phrases. 62|33. **Over-compression.** Dropped articles, verbless fragments, symbol-speak, and abbreviations that make the reader decode instead of read. 14|| Discriminated unions | Model variants with a `kind` literal discriminant so impossible states can't be represented. No optional-field bags. |
15|| Branded types | Brand primitives with `& { readonly __brand: "X" }` so they can't be mixed up. Validate once at the boundary. A brand comes from a verifying type guard (`input is AgentId`), never from `as`. |
16|| Constructive modeling | Build the shape so the illegal value can't be constructed. `[T, ...T[]]` for non-empty, `[T, T][]` for even length, `start` plus `duration` for a range. Not a runtime guard, not a wish for refinement types. |
17|| Simplest total type | Keep `T[]` while every operation on it stays total. Strengthen to `NonEmpty<T>` only where the loose type forces `!`, a cast, or a "should never happen" throw. |
18|| `unknown` over `any` | External data is `unknown`. |
19|| Schemas before guards | Before hand-writing a property-by-property type guard, use the repository's runtime schema library and infer the type from the schema, such as `z.infer`. |
20|| No `as` casts | Every `as` is a runtime crash waiting. Cast only after validation. |
21|| Narrowing hierarchy | Discriminant switch > `in` operator > `typeof`/`instanceof` > user-defined type guard > `as`. |
22|| Type guards | Must verify the claim. A lying guard is worse than `as` because the bug hides behind a name that says it's safe. Name them `isX` or `hasX`. |
23|| Exhaustiveness | Inline `const _exhaustive: never = x;` in default arms so the compiler errors when a new variant is added. |
24|| `satisfies` over `as` | Validates the value without widening literal types. |
25|| Boundary validation | Parse where data crosses in, into a named domain type. `Record<string, unknown>` (however spelled) stops at that parse. Trust types inside. See the **boundary-discipline** principle skill. |

6|
7|# Test Behavior, Not Implementation
8|
9|A test is a claim about what the code does for its users: a caller, an end user, or another service. Behavior is what those users can observe through the interface they use. That includes return values, errors, state they can read back, and effects on systems outside the code, such as a request sent, a row written, or a message emitted. Implementation is what they cannot observe: private helpers, internal call order, intermediate data, and which internal collaborator did the work.
10|
11|Judge each test against two imagined edits:
12|
13|- **Break the behavior.** Make the code return a wrong value, skip an effect, or do the effect twice. If the test still passes, it proves nothing. The usual causes are an assertion looser than the contract, an expected value computed by the code under test, a restated constant or prompt string that never runs the code that reads it, and an assertion on data that the test built itself.
14|- **Change the internals.** Keep every observable result the same and restructure the code underneath. If the test now fails, it is pinned to the implementation. It will need a rewrite on every refactor and still catches no bug.
15|
16|Keep a test that catches the first edit and survives the second. Rewrite or delete the rest. To write a test that does both, drive the code through its users' interface with a concrete input. Derive the expected value from the requirement, not from a run of the code. Assert what the contract promises, no less and no more.
17|
18|The contract decides, not the shape of the assertion. When "an empty cart never charges" is the promise, an assertion that the payment client got no call is behavior. Pair it with a case where the charge happens, so that the test shows it can see a call. The payload that a mocked external service receives is behavior, because that service observes it. A call to an internal helper is implementation, because no user can see it. An empty list is the exact answer when no record matches, and a hollow check when the test only needs some result. An exact error message pins wording that no caller reads. The error type that callers branch on is the contract.

8|# TypeScript best practices
9|
10|Apply the **type-system-discipline** principle skill first.
11|
12|| Rule | Summary |
13||------|---------|
14|| Discriminated unions | Model variants with a `kind` literal discriminant so impossible states can't be represented. No optional-field bags. |
15|| Branded types | Brand primitives with `& { readonly __brand: "X" }` so they can't be mixed up. Validate once at the boundary. A brand comes from a verifying type guard (`input is AgentId`), never from `as`. |
16|| Constructive modeling | Build the shape so the illegal value can't be constructed. `[T, ...T[]]` for non-empty, `[T, T][]` for even length, `start` plus `duration` for a range. Not a runtime guard, not a wish for refinement types. |
17|| Simplest total type | Keep `T[]` while every operation on it stays total. Strengthen to `NonEmpty<T>` only where the loose type forces `!`, a cast, or a "should never happen" throw. |
18|| `unknown` over `any` | External data is `unknown`. |
19|| Schemas before guards | Before hand-writing a property-by-property type guard, use the repository's runtime schema library and infer the type from the schema, such as `z.infer`. |
20|| No `as` casts | Every `as` is a runtime crash waiting. Cast only after validation. |
21|| Narrowing hierarchy | Discriminant switch > `in` operator > `typeof`/`instanceof` > user-defined type guard > `as`. |
22|| Type guards | Must verify the claim. A lying guard is worse than `as` because the bug hides behind a name that says it's safe. Name them `isX` or `hasX`. |
23|| Exhaustiveness | Inline `const _exhaustive: never = x;` in default arms so the compiler errors when a new variant is added. |
24|| `satisfies` over `as` | Validates the value without widening literal types. |
25|| Boundary validation | Parse where data crosses in, into a named domain type. `Record<string, unknown>` (however spelled) stops at that parse. Trust types inside. See the **boundary-discipline** principle skill. |
26|| Schema-derived types | Reach for `Pick`/`Omit`/`Parameters`/`ReturnType`/`Awaited`/`typeof` before declaring a new interface. |
27|| Object args | Pass objects, not positional, so argument order is self-documenting. Skip on hot paths (per-frame render, tokenizers, parsers). |
28|| Real tests | Don't mock what you can run. Prefer the framework's real test primitives with leak/disposable checks, and verify UI in a running build. Mock only what you can't run locally. |
29|| Structured telemetry | Prefer structured logger diagnostics with enough context to debug from an id. No `console.log` in shipped code. |
30|

6|
7|# Unslop
8|
9|Edit text to remove AI patterns. Scan for the patterns below, then rewrite. Preserve meaning and match the intended tone.
10|
11|## Patterns to detect and fix
12|
13|Rule numbers are stable ids that other skills cite. A removed rule leaves a gap.
14|
15|### Content
16|
17|3. **Superficial -ing phrases.** "highlighting...", "ensuring...", "reflecting...", "showcasing...", "fostering...". Delete or expand with real sources.
18|5. **Vague attributions.** "Experts believe", "Industry reports suggest", "Some critics argue". Name the source or delete.
19|
20|### Language
21|
22|7. **AI vocabulary.** Additionally, crucial, delve, enduring, enhance, fostering, garner, interplay, intricate, landscape (abstract), pivotal, showcase, tapestry (abstract), testament, underscore, vibrant. Replace with plain words.
23|8. **Fancy ways to say "is".** "serves as", "stands as", "boasts", "features". Say "is" or "has".
24|9. **"Not just X, but Y."** State the point directly instead.
25|10. **Rule of three.** Don't force ideas into groups of three. Use the natural number.
26|11. **Synonym cycling.** Protagonist, main character, central figure, hero all in one paragraph. Pick one, repeat it.
27|12. **False ranges.** "from X to Y" where X and Y aren't on a meaningful scale. List topics directly.
28|
29|### Style
30|
31|13. **Em dash overuse.** Avoid em dashes entirely. Use periods or commas only (no parentheses, no en dashes, no hyphen-as-dash substitutes). If a thought needs separation, end the sentence or use a comma.
32|14. **Colon overuse.** Colons are fine before a list or example, not as mid-sentence connectors. "If you're coming from traditional automation: instead of registering event handlers, you describe conditions" adds nothing with the colon. Rewrite to let the point stand on its own without comparison framing. "Describing when the scheduler should fire works best as plain English." Same meaning, no crutch punctuation.
33|15. **Boldface overuse.** Don't bold every proper noun or acronym.
34|16. **Inline-header lists.** The tell is a bold label and colon that restates the line: "**Performance:** Performance improved...". Convert those to prose. A bold lead-in that ends in a period, names the item, and is followed by genuinely new detail ("**Schema in TypeScript.** Tables live in one file.") is fine, not a tell.
35|17. **Title case headings.** Use sentence case.
36|18. **Decorative emojis.** Remove from headings and bullets.
37|19. **Curly quotes.** Use straight quotes.
38|
39|### Communication artifacts
40|
41|20. **Chatbot phrases.** "I hope this helps!", "Let me know if...", "Of course!", "Certainly!", "Found the smoking gun!" Remove.
42|22. **Sycophantic tone.** "Great question! You're absolutely right!" Respond directly.
43|
44|### Filler
45|
46|23. **Filler phrases.** "In order to" becomes "To". "Due to the fact that" becomes "Because". Delete "It is important to note that".
47|24. **Excessive hedging.** "could potentially possibly be argued that it might" becomes "may".
48|25. **Generic conclusions.** "The future looks bright." State specific plans or facts.
49|
50|### Jargon
51|
52|26. **Abstract metaphor nouns.** Substrate (base), wedge, wedge in (add), vector (way, method), locus, vantage, nexus, primitive as a noun, harness as a metaphor, surface as in "API surface", bedrock, scaffolding as a metaphor, modality, paradigm, gold-plating (more than the job needs), ratchet as a metaphor (the mechanism's real name, or a limit that only tightens), evacuate for moving code (move out), endgame (the last phase), north star, flywheel. These read as technical but usually have a plainer concrete word. Pick the concrete word.
53|
54|### Plain speech
55|
56|27. **Say what it does, not how it feels.** "the database stays close at hand", "SQL you can read", "types that follow your schema" name a feeling. The fix names the mechanism or a number: "`.toSQL()` returns the exact string sent to the database", "a column rename fails the build". Ask what the sentence tells the reader to do or know, then write that. If you can't restate it as a concrete instruction, fact, or number, cut it. One more check: if the sentence could appear unchanged in another project's docs, it says nothing about this one. Cut it.
57|28. **Shorten or split dense sentences.** If the reader has to backtrack to parse a sentence, break it in two or drop clauses. One idea per sentence.
58|29. **Active voice.** Prefer it. Catch "is/are/was/were + past participle" and name the actor: "queries are validated" becomes "the compiler validates queries", "the file is parsed by the loader" becomes "the loader parses the file". Passive is fine only when the actor is unknown or genuinely doesn't matter.
59|30. **Cut adverbs, or use a stronger verb.** "runs quickly" becomes "is fast" or the number, and "significantly improves" becomes the measured delta. An adverb propping up a weak verb means the verb is wrong.
60|31. **Prefer the plain word.** "utilize" and "leverage" become "use", "facilitate" becomes "help", "numerous" becomes "many", "in the event that" becomes "if". The fancier synonym is rarely clearer.
61|32. **Mannered prose.** Metaphor or flourish where a literal phrase exists: aphorisms ("wire it or delete it"), rhetorical fragments for effect, personified code ("the plan holds it"), figurative verbs ("rides along", "stands on"), stock framing phrases. "A dial worth turning" becomes "a parameter worth varying". Say what you mean. Rule 26 covers the metaphor nouns.
62|33. **Over-compression.** Dropped articles, verbless fragments, symbol-speak, and abbreviations that make the reader decode instead of read. Write whole sentences with their articles and verbs, and spell out arrows and abbreviations.

# Contracts

Music generation must never block the reader. Each module below owns one
job and can be swapped without touching the others. Import direction is
`core <- server` and `core <- app`. Server and client components never
import each other. `app/page.tsx` may import `server/books.ts`. Client
files never do.

## Book data

`data/books/oz/book.json` holds the frozen text: id, title, author,
`textVersion` hash, chapters with `start_n` and `end_n`, and paragraphs
with `id`, `ch`, `n`, and `text`. `analysis.json` is the scene source
the reader consumes: the same scenes plus Jev vectors, the Muse
override, and the `final` emotion. `scenes.json` is the pipeline
intermediate that `analysis.json` mirrors. The reader consumes the book
fields, scene ranges and titles, and the `final` vector with intensity
and tempo. It never sees `jev`, `muse_override`, or provenance.
`core/reader.ts` defines `buildReaderModel`, which joins paragraphs to
scenes by ordinal range and throws on unordered scenes or on paragraphs
covered zero or two times.

## Scene reader

One static route per scene (`app/leer/[sceneId]`, `dynamicParams`
false); `/` redirects to the first scene. The layout mounts the music
container once and passes slim metadata for all scenes: id, chapter,
and emotion triple only. Each scene page builds its view with
`buildSceneView` and ships only that scene's text, its chapter title,
and neighbor ids. Sub-pages come from `paginateScene` (250 words, split
at paragraph boundaries). The pager moves sub-pages in client state and
pushes routes with `router.push`, never `<Link>`; going back lands on
the previous scene's last sub-page through a one-shot client flag, never
a URL param, so prerendered pages stay static. The client never
receives other scenes' text, titles, or summaries.

## Music library

The library is a static `public/music/manifest.json`, version 3, fetched
by the client from `/music/manifest.json`. A static file needs no route,
ships from the CDN, and swaps by replacing files only. Tracks may be
several minutes long and are not loops unless marked so. A version 2
manifest migrates inline to one implicit `default` soundtrack of style
`orchestral`.

`MusicManifest = { version, styles, soundtracks, tracks, playlists }`.
`StyleInfo = { id, name }` where `id` is a lowercase slug and `name` is
the Spanish display name. `Soundtrack = { id, name, style }` plus
optional `credit`. `Track = { id, src, title, emotion, vector,
intensity, tempo, durationSec, soundtrack, style }` plus optional
`startSec` (default 0, where playback starts on first play and on each
loop), `loop` (default true), `source` (`generated`, `jamendo`, or
`recording`), `artist`, `composer`, `license`, `attribution`, and
`sourceUrl` (https only). `emotion` is the hand label: one of the 8
emotion ids in `core/types.ts`. The vector covers the 8 ids with finite
entries in 0..1. Every track names a soundtrack id, every track style
matches its soundtrack style, and every style is a listed style id.
`core/music.ts` owns `parseManifest`, which rejects unknown versions,
duplicate ids, unknown soundtrack or style ids, style mismatches,
missing fields, bad vectors, NaN entries, out-of-range numbers,
`startSec` outside its range, unknown `source` values, a non-boolean
`playlistOnly`, and any `src`
that is not a `/music/` path or `https` URL. A soundtrack with no
tracks parses. The reader calls it on every fetch, so a bad drop-in
fails loudly in dev. Remote URLs need a `media-src` addition in
`next.config.ts`.

`Track.playlistOnly` defaults to false. A true value marks a playlist
only track: it still names a soundtrack and style, but no emotion pick
ever returns it. `MusicManifest.playlists` holds
`Playlist = { id, label, trackIds }` entries, most notably
`just-play-chopin`. A missing key parses as an empty list, and a v2
migration gives an empty list. Parse rejects duplicate playlist ids,
empty labels, non-array `trackIds`, and any `trackIds` entry that names
no track, with the playlist and the id in the message.

## Soundtracks and selection

One soundtrack plays at a time. `MusicSelection = { mode, soundtrackId,
style }` is the session: `style` scopes every pick, `soundtrackId` is
the home in `soundtrack` mode, `mode` picks the ranking rule. The style
is the user's choice, changed with the style selector. The initial
soundtrack is the one covering the most hand-labeled emotions, ties by
lower id; a valid persisted id wins. The session persists `{ mode,
soundtrackId, style }` in localStorage under `lectoria.music.v1`. On
load a stored style with no tracks and a stored soundtrack outside the
stored style fall back to the defaults. Storage exceptions never break
playback.

In `soundtrack` mode each scene scores only the session soundtrack. When
the soundtrack has no track with the scene emotion, the scheduler borrows
the best same-style track for that scene only and reports `fallback`, so
the bar can say `de otra banda sonora`. In `random` mode each scheduled
select draws among same-style tracks with the scene emotion (or the best
same-style tracks when the emotion is missing) within `randomTolerance`
(0.05) of the best score, keeps the current track when it is eligible,
and avoids an immediate repeat otherwise. Dwell and min-track rules hold
in both modes. The core never calls `Math.random`; the reader injects it
and tests pass a seeded stub.

## Change track, mix toggle, style change

`nextTrack` cycles same-emotion tracks in score order, wrapping and
skipping the current. In `soundtrack` mode it stays inside the current
soundtrack first, then tries the same emotion in other same-style
soundtracks, then the best same-style track overall. In `random` mode it
ranges over all same-style soundtracks at once. A null scene cycles the
style set in id order.

The `Mezclar bandas` toggle flips `mode`. Turning it off keeps the
soundtrack of the playing track. `requestStyleChange` moves the session
to the best-coverage soundtrack of the new style and picks the best
match for the scene inside that soundtrack, or the best same-style track
by score when the picked soundtrack lacks the scene emotion. It never
crosses styles. The scheduler applies it at once with the normal
crossfade and holds the choice like a Next. There is no
soundtrack-change button.

101|## Change track, mix toggle, style change
102|
103|`nextTrack` cycles same-emotion tracks in score order, wrapping and
104|skipping the current. In `soundtrack` mode it stays inside the current
105|soundtrack first, then tries the same emotion in other same-style
106|soundtracks, then the best same-style track overall. In `random` mode it
107|ranges over all same-style soundtracks at once. A null scene cycles the
108|style set in id order.
109|
110|The `Mezclar bandas` toggle flips `mode`. Turning it off keeps the
111|soundtrack of the playing track. `requestStyleChange` moves the session
112|to the best-coverage soundtrack of the new style and picks the best
113|match for the scene inside that soundtrack, or the best same-style track
114|by score when the picked soundtrack lacks the scene emotion. It never
115|crosses styles. The scheduler applies it at once with the normal
116|crossfade and holds the choice like a Next. There is no
117|soundtrack-change button.
118|
119|## Playlist mode
120|
121|`SchedulerState.playlist` holds `{ id, index }` while a fixed playlist
122|plays. `enterPlaylist` switches at once to the first `trackIds` entry
123|with `crossfadeSec`, no dwell and no min-track rule. While it is on,
124|scene changes update the active scene but never switch, `requestNext`
125|and `noteTrackEnded` advance to the next entry in order and wrap from
126|the last to the first, and playlist tracks run to their end because the
127|player forces looping off. `exitPlaylist` clears the playlist state and
128|switches at once to the best match for the current scene under the
129|restored selection. The mode is never persisted, so a reload returns to
130|emotion mode. The mix toggle and the style selector stay disabled while
131|it is on, and the style list hides styles with only playlist tracks.
132|
133|## Similarity and config
134|
135|`Similarity = (scene, track, weights) => number`, where
136|`SceneSignal = { vector, intensity, tempo }`. The default is
137|`bhattacharyyaSimilarity`: both 8-emotion vectors renormalize to sum 1
138|(an all-zero vector gives an affinity of 0), `E` is the sum of
139|`sqrt(s_k * t_k)`, and the score is `weights.emotion * E` plus
140|`weights.intensity` and `weights.tempo` each for intensity and tempo
141|closeness. Scoring and ranking pass the resolved config weights in, so
142|a weights override changes the ranking. `cosineSimilarity` over
143|`buildFeatures` output stays as an exported alternative. One exported object,
144|`MUSIC_CONFIG`, holds `similarity`, `weights`, `switchMargin` (0.07),
145|`dwellSec` (20), `minTrackSec` (45), `hardCutMargin` (0.20),
146|`crossfadeSec` (3), and `hardCutCrossfadeSec` (1.5). Everything else
147|reads from it. Ranking ties go to the lower track id. Route entries use
148|`sceneEntryDwellSec` (5) as the dwell override; scoring, hysteresis,
149|and overrides are unchanged.
150|
151|## Selection scheduler
152|
153|`core/music-schedule.ts` is a pure state machine. The reader calls
154|`observeScene`, `tickScheduler`, `requestNext`, and `noteTrackEnded`
155|with explicit `nowSec` values, so all timing is testable without
156|timers. The reader cues music on scene entry only: one `observeScene`
157|call per route id, gated by an id comparison, so sub-page moves never
158|reach the scheduler. State holds the current track id and when it started, the active
159|scene id, the pending scene id and since when, and the skip override
160|with the scene it belongs to.
161|
162|A newly entered scene becomes pending and the dwell clock restarts, so
163|fast scrolling keeps only the newest scene. The first track ever plays
164|at once with no dwell. After the pending scene holds for `dwellSec` it
165|becomes active and the override clears. Then the best track switches in
166|only when it beats the current score by `switchMargin` and the current
167|track played `minTrackSec`, unless it wins by `hardCutMargin` (hard
168|cut, short fade). A second passes the active scene back through the
169|switch check, so a hold from `minTrackSec` releases on time, unless a
170|skip override stands: ticks return no change while it is set, and only
171|a new scene promotion clears it. A switch
172|reports its crossfade length: 3 s normally,
173|1.5 s for hard cuts. The skip choice holds until the next scene change;
174|after that, dwell and hysteresis apply with the override track as the
175|current track. A null scene means a failed analysis with no vector, so
176|it never triggers a switch. A non-looping track that ends fades into
177|the best remaining track, excluding the one that ended, and clears the
178|skip override.
179|
180|## Player
181|
182|`app/player.tsx` takes the track, the fade length for the latest switch,
183|the scene title, a skip flag, and callbacks. It owns two `audio`
184|elements, play state, volume, and the equal-power crossfade
185|(cos/sin gains over the fade time, driven by `requestAnimationFrame`).
186|It never uses the `loop` attribute. Volume lives in a ref, so the slider
187|never re-runs the track effect or touches `src`. A new track request
188|mid-fade cancels the pending fade and fades from the audible element to
189|the newest track. On load each track seeks to `startSec` once metadata
190|is available. Long tracks with `loop` true crossfade into the other
191|element playing the same track from `startSec` when `currentTime`
192|reaches `duration - fade`, where `fade` is the latest scheduler fade
193|length, or the config `crossfadeSec` when none was reported yet. When
194|`loop` is false the player reports the end and the scheduler picks the
195|next-best track excluding the ended one. Pause stops both elements and
196|freezes the fade in place; play resumes the audible elements from the
197|frozen point. Audio starts once, on the first press, with fade 0.
198|Audio starts only after the user presses play. Reduced motion is read in
199|state with a change listener and affects visuals only, never the fade.
200|
201|The bar shows Play/Pause, Volume, a Cambiar track button (disabled when
202|Next has nothing to offer), a Mezclar bandas toggle with `aria-pressed`,
203|and a style selector listing only styles that have tracks (hidden while
204|fewer than two qualify). A `Just play Chopin` toggle appears only when
205|the manifest defines that playlist with tracks; its text comes from the
206|playlist label, it carries `aria-pressed`, and it shows the Meta blue
207|accent while pressed. It shows the track title with its emotion
208|label, the soundtrack name, and attribution when present: composer or
209|artist, license, and a source link. While the playlist plays, the bar
210|hides the emotion label and the fallback note. A fallback pick adds the
211|quiet note
212|`de otra banda sonora`. On manifest failure the reader still renders and
213|the bar shows a short neutral note. UI motion stays under 200 ms.
214|Controls are real buttons and inputs with labels, visible focus, and
215|keyboard use. `app/player.tsx` keeps the audio engine and bar layout;
216|`app/player-controls.tsx` holds the buttons and the style selector;
217|`app/music-prefs.ts` owns the storage helper.
218|
219|## Image api
220|
221|`POST /api/images` (Node runtime, `maxDuration` 120). Request is a
222|discriminated union: `{ kind: "passage", bookId, textVersion, n }` names
223|the paragraph where the selection starts, `{ kind: "scene", bookId,
224|textVersion, sceneId }` names the scene. Validation is strict: known
225|book, matching `textVersion`, integer `n` inside the book, known
226|`sceneId`. Any other body is a 400 with a generic Spanish message.
227|The client sends ordinals and ids only, never text. "Ilustrar
228|escena" uses the scene id from the route.
229|
230|Responses (typed in `core/types.ts`): `{ status: "ready", url, cached,
231|caption }` with a Vercel Blob URL, never bytes; `{ status: "pending" }`
232|when another request holds the lock, in which case the client reposts
233|every 3 s up to about 2 minutes; `{ status: "error", code, message }`
234|where code is `quota`, `budget`, `unavailable`, or `bad_request` with a
235|friendly Spanish message. Caption is the scene title for scenes and the
236|first words of the paragraph for passages, built server-side.
237|
238|The passage cache key is book plus start paragraph plus `textVersion`
239|plus `PROMPT_VERSION` (`v1`); the scene key is book plus scene id plus
240|the same versions. Both map to a deterministic Blob path
241|(`addRandomSuffix: false`, `allowOverwrite: false`). An Upstash Redis
242|index maps key to Blob URL, so hits are one GET; on an index miss the
243|server lists by exact path prefix (head equivalent) before generating
244|and backfills the index.
245|A Redis lock per key returns `pending` to concurrent requests. Quota is
246|5 new images per person per day by hashed IP and signed cookie,
247|whichever runs out first; a shared spend counter in integer
248|micro-dollars sits under `SPEND_CAP_USD` (default 10). Failures refund
249|quota and budget and release the lock.
250|
251|## Chat api
252|
253|Contract only, no routes. Request `{ bookId, textVersion, positionN,
254|spoilerMode, messages }` carries the chat history and the reader
255|position. The response is streamed text. The server builds context from
256|the book text up to `positionN`, or the whole book when `spoilerMode` is
257|on, with the book prefix first and the question last so readers share
258|the prompt cache. The system prompt answers only from that text and
259|refuses the rest. Types live in `core/types.ts`.
260|
261|## Quotas and budget
262|
263|Server only. Spend is counted in integer micro-dollars: reserve with
264|Redis `INCRBY` before each model call, refund with `DECRBY` after, one
265|reserve per call including retries. The server clamps every model tool
266|argument. Clients never see keys or raw errors. Generic messages go to
267|the client, details stay in server logs.
